results.title: Completely multiplicative arithmetic function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $R$ be a type with a multiplication and a zero. An arithmetic function $f$ with values in $R$ (so $f(0) = 0$) is completely multiplicative if $f(mn) = f(m) f(n)$ for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$.

results.title: Completely multiplicative functions preserve products
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a type with a multiplication and a zero, and let $f$ be a completely multiplicative arithmetic function with values in $R$. Then $f(mn) = f(m) f(n)$ for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$.

results.title: Normalized completely multiplicative functions are multiplicative
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a monoid with zero and let $f$ be a completely multiplicative arithmetic function with values in $R$ such that $f(1) = 1$. Then $f$ is multiplicative: $f(1) = 1$ and $f(mn) = f(m) f(n)$ for all coprime natural numbers $m$ and $n$.

results.title: Binary code of a subset
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$ and a subset $A$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$, the binary code of $A$ is the natural number $b(A) = \sum_{i \in A} 2^i$.

results.title: Set order
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For subsets $A$ and $B$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, $A$ precedes $B$ in the set order, written $A < B$, if $|A| > |B|$, or $|A| = |B|$ and $b(A) < b(B)$, where $b(A) = \sum_{i \in A} 2^i$ is the binary code of $A$.

results.title: Sort key of a subset
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a subset $A$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the sort key of $A$ is the natural number $(n - |A|) \cdot 2^n + b(A)$, where $b(A) = \sum_{i \in A} 2^i$ is the binary code of $A$.

results.title: String of a family
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a family $U$ of subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the string $s(U)$ is the list of the sort keys of the nonempty members of $U$, in increasing order.

results.title: Permuted image of a family
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a family $U$ of subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the permuted image $\sigma(U)$ is the family $\{\sigma(A) : A \in U\}$, where $\sigma(A) = \{\sigma(a) : a \in A\}$.

results.title: Union-closed family
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A family $U$ of subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is union-closed if $A \cup B \in U$ for all $A, B \in U$.

results.title: Canonical family
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A family $U$ of subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is canonical, the canonical representative of its isomorphism class, if for every permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ the string $s(U)$ is lexicographically at most the string $s(\sigma(U))$ of the permuted family $\sigma(U)$.

results.title: The sort key encodes the set order

results.summary: For all subsets $A$ and $B$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, $A < B$ in the set order if and only if the sort key of $A$ is less than the sort key of $B$.

results.title: Decoding a literal
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a bit string $w$, the decoder reads a prefix-coded natural number $n$ from the front of $w$ and then one more bit $b$. results.title: Codes with empty domain
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The set $E$ consists of the codes $c$ of partial recursive functions on $\mathbb{N}$ that are defined on no input: for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the function computed by $c$ is undefined at $n$.

results.title: Emptiness is undecidable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The set $E$ of codes of partial recursive functions on $\mathbb{N}$ that are defined on no input is not decidable by multi-stack machines.

results.title: Nonemptiness is recognizable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The set of codes of partial recursive functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that are defined on at least one input is recognizable by multi-stack machines: some multi-stack machine halts on the binary encoding of a code $c$ exactly when the function coded by $c$ is defined on some input.

results.title: Emptiness is co-recognizable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The set of codes of partial recursive functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that are defined on no input is co-recognizable by multi-stack machines: some multi-stack machine halts on the binary encoding of a code $c$ exactly when the function coded by $c$ is defined on at least one input.

results.title: Emptiness is not recognizable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The set $E$ of codes of partial recursive functions on $\mathbb{N}$ that are defined on no input is not recognizable by multi-stack machines: no multi-stack machine, started on the binary encoding of a code, halts exactly when the code is in $E$.

results.title: Equivalent codes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The set $EQ$ consists of the pairs $(c_1, c_2)$ of codes of partial recursive functions on $\mathbb{N}$ that recognize the same language, that is, whose computed functions have the same domain: for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the function computed by $c_1$ is defined at $n$ if and only if the function computed by $c_2$ is.

results.title: A code defined nowhere
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is a code $e$ of a partial recursive function on $\mathbb{N}$ whose computed function is the empty partial function, undefined at every input.

results.title: Emptiness reduces to equivalence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The set $E$ of codes of partial recursive functions defined on no input is many-one reducible to the set $EQ$ of pairs of codes with the same domain: there is a computable map $f$ from codes to pairs of codes such that, for every code $c$, $c \in E$ if and only if $f(c) \in EQ$.

results.title: Equivalence is not recognizable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The set $EQ$ of pairs of codes of partial recursive functions on $\mathbb{N}$ with the same domain is not recognizable by multi-stack machines: no multi-stack machine, started on the binary encoding of a pair of codes, halts exactly when the pair is in $EQ$.

results.title: Halting-on-zero code
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a code $c$ of a partial recursive function on $\mathbb{N}$, the code $h(c)$ is the composition $k_0 \circ c \circ k_0$, where $k_0$ is the code of the constant function $0$: whatever its input, $h(c)$ runs $c$ on $0$ and, if this halts, outputs $0$.

results.title: Halting on zero reduces to equivalence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The set of codes $c$ of partial recursive functions on $\mathbb{N}$ that halt on input $0$ (are defined at $0$) is many-one reducible to the set $EQ$ of pairs of codes with the same domain: there is a computable map $f$ from codes to pairs of codes such that, for every code $c$, $c$ halts on $0$ if and only if $f(c) \in EQ$.

results.title: Equivalence is not co-recognizable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The set $EQ$ of pairs of codes of partial recursive functions on $\mathbb{N}$ with the same domain is not co-recognizable by multi-stack machines: no multi-stack machine, started on the binary encoding of a pair of codes, halts exactly when the pair is not in $EQ$.

results.summary: Given for each receiver $w$ a ranking $\sigma_w$ of the $n$ proposers (a permutation of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, with $\sigma_w(0)$ her first choice), the receivers' preference profile assigns to $w$ the preference order of $\sigma_w$: $w$ prefers $a$ to $b$ when $\sigma_w^{-1}(a) < \sigma_w^{-1}(b)$.

results.title: Deferred-acceptance state
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A state of deferred acceptance with $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers, both numbered $0, \dots, n-1$, records for each proposer a natural number, the number of proposals he has made (his next proposal goes to his choice of that rank), and for each receiver either the proposer she currently holds or that she holds nobody.

results.title: Initial state of deferred acceptance
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The initial state with $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers: every proposer has made $0$ proposals and no receiver holds anyone.

results.title: Free proposer
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A proposer $m$ is free in a state $s$ of deferred acceptance when no receiver holds $m$ in $s$.

results.title: Receiver's holder after a proposal
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In a state $s$ of deferred acceptance, the proposer whom receiver $w$ holds after proposer $m$ proposes to her is $m$ if she holds nobody in $s$ or ranks $m$ strictly better than her current holder $m'$ in her ranking, and $m'$ otherwise.

results.title: Choosing the next proposer
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In a state $s$ of deferred acceptance with proposers $0, 1, \dots, n-1$, the chooser returns the least proposer $m$ who is free in $s$ and has made fewer than $n$ proposals in $s$, or no proposer if there is none.

results.title: Running deferred acceptance
results.caption: Definition

Starting from a state $s$ with a budget of $f$ proposals: if $f = 0$, or if no proposer is both free (held by no receiver) and has made fewer than $n$ proposals, the run returns $s$; otherwise the lowest-numbered such proposer makes a proposal, and the run continues from the resulting state with budget $f - 1$.

results.title: Remaining proposals
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a state $s$ of deferred acceptance with $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers, in which each proposer $m$ has made $k_m$ proposals, the number of proposals still available is $\sum_{m} \max(n - k_m, 0)$, the sum running over all $n$ proposers.

results.title: A proposal adds one to the proposal count
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Deferred acceptance makes at most n² proposals
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For any rankings of the $n$ receivers by each of the $n$ proposers and of the proposers by each receiver, in the final state of deferred acceptance the numbers of proposals made by the proposers sum to at most $n \cdot n$.

results.title: When deferred acceptance stops, every proposer is held
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Fix rankings of the $n$ receivers by each of $n$ proposers and of the proposers by each receiver. Let $s$ be a state of deferred acceptance that satisfies the invariant of deferred acceptance for these rankings, and suppose that no proposer is both free in $s$ and has made fewer than $n$ proposals in $s$. Then every proposer is held by some receiver in $s$.

results.title: Every receiver holds someone once every proposer is held
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a state of deferred acceptance with $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers. If every proposer is held by some receiver in $s$, then every receiver holds some proposer in $s$.

results.title: Receiver's partner
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In a state $s$ of deferred acceptance with $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers, both numbered $0, \dots, n-1$, the partner of a receiver $w$ is the proposer she holds in $s$; if she holds nobody, it is the proposer numbered $w$ (a default value).

results.title: Proposer's partner
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In a state $s$ of deferred acceptance with $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers, both numbered $0, \dots, n-1$, the partner of a proposer $m$ is the lowest-numbered receiver that holds $m$ in $s$; if no receiver holds $m$, it is the receiver numbered $m$ (a default value).

results.title: The Gale-Shapley matching is stable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers, each with a ranking of the other side, the perfect matching computed by deferred acceptance is stable for the strict preferences given by these rankings.

results.title: Proposer-optimality
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: No stable matching gives a proposer a partner he prefers to his Gale-Shapley partner.

results.title: Receiver-pessimality
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: No stable matching gives a receiver a partner she likes less than her Gale-Shapley partner.

results.title: Rank under a strict total order
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a strict total order $<$ on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the rank of an element $a$ is the number of elements $b$ with $b < a$ (the elements preferred to $a$), as an element of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$.

results.title: Every strict total order on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is given by a ranking
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every strict total order $\prec$ on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ there is a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ such that, for all $a$ and $b$, $a \prec b$ holds exactly when $\sigma^{-1}(a) < \sigma^{-1}(b)$.

results.title: Linear code
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: Let $F$ be a field and $\iota$ an index set, not necessarily finite. A linear code over $F$ with coordinates indexed by $\iota$ is an $F$-linear subspace of the space of words, the functions $\iota \to F$.

results.title: Encoder of a generator matrix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a $\kappa \times \iota$ matrix over a field $F$, with $\kappa$ finite. The encoder of $G$ sends a message $m \in F^\kappa$ to the word $mG \in F^\iota$ given by $(mG)_j = \sum_{k \in \kappa} m_k G_{kj}$, the combination of the rows of $G$ with coefficients $m$.

results.title: Code generated by a matrix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $F$ be a field, $\kappa$ a finite index set, $\iota$ any index set and $G$ a $\kappa \times \iota$ matrix over $F$. The code generated by $G$ is the linear code of all words $m G$ with $m : \kappa \to F$, the image of the encoder $m \mapsto m G$; equivalently, the span of the rows of $G$.

results.title: Syndrome
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $F$ be a field, $\iota$ a finite set and $\rho$ a set. For a matrix $H \in F^{\rho \times \iota}$ (a parity-check matrix) and a word $y \in F^\iota$, the syndrome of $y$ is the vector $Hy \in F^\rho$.

results.title: Code with a given parity-check matrix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $F$ be a field, $\iota$ a finite index set, $\rho$ any index set and $H$ a $\rho \times \iota$ matrix over $F$. The code with parity-check matrix $H$ is the linear code of all words $c : \iota \to F$ whose syndrome $H c$ is zero, that is, the kernel of $c \mapsto H c$.

results.title: The syndrome depends only on the error
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a field, $\iota$ a finite set and $H$ a parity-check matrix over $F$ with columns indexed by $\iota$. If $c \in F^\iota$ is a codeword of the code with parity-check matrix $H$ and $e \in F^\iota$ is any word, then the received word $c + e$ has the same syndrome as $e$, that is, $H(c + e) = He$.

results.title: Generator/parity-check duality
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a field, $\kappa$ and $\iota$ finite index sets and $\rho$ any index set, and let $G$ be a $\kappa \times \iota$ matrix and $H$ a $\rho \times \iota$ matrix over $F$. The code generated by $G$ equals the code with parity-check matrix $H$ if and only if $G H^{\mathsf{T}} = 0$ and $\operatorname{rank} G + \operatorname{rank} H$ equals $|\iota|$, the length of the code.

results.title: The systematic encoder copies the message
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a field, $\kappa$ a finite set and $A$ a $\kappa \times \rho$ matrix over $F$. For the systematic generator matrix $G = [I \mid A]$, whose columns are indexed by the disjoint union $\kappa \sqcup \rho$, the encoding $mG$ of every message $m \in F^\kappa$ agrees with $m$ on the coordinates in $\kappa$: $(mG)_i = m_i$ for every $i \in \kappa$.

results.title: Systematic generator and parity-check matrices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a field, $\kappa$ and $\rho$ finite sets, and $A$ a $\kappa \times \rho$ matrix over $F$. Then the code generated by $G = [I_\kappa \mid A]$ equals the code with parity-check matrix $H = [-A^{\mathsf{T}} \mid I_\rho]$, both being codes whose coordinates are indexed by the disjoint union of $\kappa$ and $\rho$.

results.title: Dot product bilinear form
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: Let $F$ be a field and $\iota$ a finite set. The dot product form is the bilinear form on $F^\iota$ that sends a pair of words $(x, y)$ to $x \cdot y = \sum_{i \in \iota} x_i y_i$.

results.title: Dual code
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $F$ be a field and $\iota$ a finite set. The dual $C^\perp$ of a linear code $C \subseteq F^\iota$ is the linear code of all words $x \in F^\iota$ with $x \cdot c = \sum_{i \in \iota} x_i c_i = 0$ for every codeword $c \in C$.

results.title: Dimension of the dual code
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a field and $\iota$ a finite set. For every linear code $C \subseteq F^\iota$, $\dim C + \dim C^\perp = |\iota|$, where $C^\perp$ is the dual code.

results.title: Dual of the code generated by a matrix
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a matrix over a field $F$ with finitely many rows and finitely many columns. Then the dual of the code generated by $G$ (the span of its rows) is the code with parity-check matrix $G$ (the words $x$ with $Gx = 0$).

results.title: Dual of the code with a given parity-check matrix
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $H$ be a matrix over a field $F$ with finitely many rows and finitely many columns. Then the dual of the code with parity-check matrix $H$ (the words $x$ with $Hx = 0$) is the code generated by $H$ (the span of its rows).

results.title: Minimum distance
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The minimum distance of a linear code $C$ of finite length is the least Hamming distance (number of coordinates where they differ) between two distinct codewords of $C$, taken in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$; it is $\infty$ if $C$ has at most one codeword.

results.title: Minimum weight
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The minimum weight of a linear code $C$ of finite length is the least weight of a nonzero codeword of $C$, where the weight of a word is its number of nonzero coordinates; it is taken in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ and is $\infty$ if $C$ has no nonzero codeword.

results.title: Hamming distance is the weight of the difference
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a field and $\iota$ a finite set. For all words $x, y \in F^\iota$, the Hamming distance between $x$ and $y$ (the number of coordinates where they differ) equals the Hamming weight of $x - y$ (its number of nonzero coordinates).

results.title: Minimum distance equals minimum weight
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a linear code of finite length over a field, the minimum distance equals the minimum weight.

results.title: Syndrome decoding
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Syndrome decoding with a lookup `table` from syndromes to error patterns: subtract the error pattern the table assigns to the syndrome of the received word.

results.title: Syndrome decoding up to half the minimum distance
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $H$ be a parity-check matrix over a field $F$ such that the code $C$ with parity-check matrix $H$ has finite minimum distance $d$, and let $t = \lfloor (d - 1)/2 \rfloor$. If a syndrome table is correct up to radius $t$ for $H$, then for every codeword $c \in C$ and every word $e$ of Hamming weight at most $t$, syndrome decoding with this table sends the received word $c + e$ to $c$.

results.title: Existence of correct syndrome tables
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $H$ be a matrix over a field $F$ whose columns are indexed by a finite set. For every natural number $t$ there is a syndrome table for $H$ that is correct up to radius $t$.

results.title: Syndrome table by exhaustive search
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $F$ be a field, $\iota$ and $\rho$ finite sets, $H$ a $\rho \times \iota$ parity-check matrix over $F$, and $t \in \mathbb{N}$, where the words $F^\iota$ come with a fixed enumeration. The search table sends a syndrome $s \in F^\rho$ to the first word $e \in F^\iota$ in the enumeration with Hamming weight at most $t$ and syndrome $He = s$, and to $0$ if there is no such word.

results.title: Number of codewords of a linear code
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $C$ is a linear code of length $n$ over a finite field $F$, then exactly $|F|^{\dim C}$ of the $|F|^n$ words of length $n$ lie in $C$, where $\dim C$ is the dimension of $C$ over $F$.

results.title: Singleton bound for linear codes, dimension form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $C$ be a linear code of length $n$ over a finite field $F$, and let $d \le n$ be a natural number that is at most the minimum distance of $C$. Then $\dim C + d \le n + 1$.

results.title: Minimum distance is at most the length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $C$ is a linear code of length $n$ over a field and $C$ is not the zero subspace, then the minimum distance of $C$ is finite and at most $n$.

results.title: Singleton bound for linear codes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a finite field and $C$ a linear code of length $n$ and dimension $k$ over $F$ that is not the zero subspace. Then the minimum distance of $C$ is at most $n - k + 1$.
